title: Decision Logic, Short-Circuit Evaluation & Pattern Matching
summary: Learn boolean truthiness, short-circuit evaluation guarantees, guards, and Python 3.10+ structural pattern matching.
learningObjectives: Leverage boolean short-circuit mechanics to guard against null/empty pointer exceptions
Write clean, readable branch controllers using structural pattern matching (match/case) with guards

sections.heading: 1. Boolean Mechanics, Short-Circuiting & Pattern Matching
sections.content:
Every object in Python possesses an inherent boolean truth value. When passed to `bool(x)` or tested in an `if` statement, an object evaluates to `False` if it is:
- A built-in constant: `None`, `False`
- Zero of any numeric type: `0`, `0.0`, `Decimal(0)`
- Any empty sequence or collection: `''`, `()`, `[]`, `{}`, `set()`

All other objects evaluate to `True`.

Python guarantees left-to-right short-circuit evaluation:
- In `expr_a and expr_b`: if `expr_a` is falsy, Python immediately returns `expr_a` WITHOUT evaluating `expr_b`.
- In `expr_a or expr_b`: if `expr_a` is truthy, Python immediately returns `expr_a` WITHOUT evaluating `expr_b`.

This guarantee allows engineers to write safe guards: `if user and user.is_authenticated():` will never crash with an AttributeError even if `user` is None.

Furthermore, Python 3.10 introduced Structural Pattern Matching (`match`/`case`). Unlike C-style switch statements, pattern matching unpacks sequences, extracts dictionary keys, and evaluates type signatures with conditional guards simultaneously.

codeExamples.code:
+-------------------------------------------------------------------+
| SHORT-CIRCUIT EVALUATION & STRUCTURAL PATTERN MATCHING            |
|                                                                   |
|  [expr_a] --- If False ---> Stop & return False (AND circuit)     |
|      |                                                            |
|    If True                                                        |
|      v                                                            |
|  [expr_b] evaluated safely (e.g. user.get_profile())               |
|                                                                   |
|  Structural Pattern Matching (match / case):                      |
|  match response:                                                  |
|    case {"status": 200, "data": [*items]} if len(items) > 0: ... |
|    case {"status": 404, "error": msg}: ...                        |
|    case _: ... (Default fallback)                                 |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------+
codeExamples.explanation: Short-circuiting skips unnecessary right-hand evaluations, while pattern matching deconstructs complex nested data structures with guards.

keyPoints: Empty collections and numeric zeros are falsy; all other objects are truthy by default.
Short-circuit evaluation guarantees safe attribute chaining without explicit nested if checks.
match/case inspects shapes of data, extracting variables and applying 'if' guards declaratively.
commonMistakes: Writing 'if x == True:' instead of idiomatic 'if x:' or 'if x is True:'.
Evaluating functions with side effects on the right side of 'or'/'and', unaware they may never execute.

sections.heading: 2. Production Request Router using Structural Pattern Matching
sections.content: Production microservices often ingest polymorphic JSON event payloads from message brokers (Kafka/RabbitMQ). Replacing tangled if-elif-else trees with structural pattern matching enhances maintainability and catches malformed message shapes immediately.

codeExamples.code:
def route_event(event: dict) -> str:
    """Route microservice event payloads using structural pattern matching."""
    match event:
        case {"type": "ORDER_CREATED", "payload": {"order_id": int(oid), "amount": float(amt)}} if amt > 0:
            return f"Processing valid order #{oid} for {amt:.2f} USD"
            
        case {"type": "ORDER_CREATED", "payload": {"amount": float(amt)}} if amt <= 0:
            return "Rejected: Order amount must be positive"
            
        case {"type": "USER_SIGNUP", "payload": {"email": str(email)}} if "@" in email:
            return f"Provisioning account for {email}"
            
        case {"type": str(event_type), "error": str(err_msg)}:
            return f"Alert: Failure in {event_type} - {err_msg}"
            
        case _:
            return "Rejected: Unrecognized or malformed event schema"

# Testing event routes
print(route_event({"type": "ORDER_CREATED", "payload": {"order_id": 1042, "amount": 89.50}}))
print(route_event({"type": "USER_SIGNUP", "payload": {"email": "dev@careertwin.ai"}}))
print(route_event({"type": "INVALID_SCHEMA"}))
codeExamples.explanation: Demonstrates pattern matching with type assertions, dictionary destructuring, and conditional guards.
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
Processing valid order #1042 for $89.50
Provisioning account for dev@careertwin.ai
Rejected: Unrecognized or malformed event schema

keyPoints: The wildcard pattern `_` acts as a mandatory catch-all default to ensure no event is dropped silently.
Guards (`if amt > 0`) allow business rules to be validated directly in the pattern definition.
commonMistakes: Forgetting that pattern matching evaluates cases sequentially from top to bottom; putting general cases first masks specific cases.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: What will the expression 'None and print("Hello")' output?

options.text: It prints nothing and evaluates to None due to short-circuit evaluation.
It raises a TypeError because None cannot be combined with a function call.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Because None is falsy, the 'and' operator short-circuits immediately without evaluating the right operand.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: In Python 3.10+ structural pattern matching, what is the role of the '_' pattern?

options.text: It declares a private local variable.
It acts as a wildcard catch-all pattern matching any value.
It forces the match statement to loop back to the beginning.
It ignores whitespace in string matching.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: The wildcard '_' matches any value and is commonly used as the default branch at the end of a match block.

recap: Short-circuit boolean logic enables safe property evaluation. Python 3.10+ pattern matching provides structural destructuring with guards, eliminating verbose nested condition chains.
